title: The Changing Economic World: Nigeria
examTip: Nigeria is an NEE, not an LIC — always use this classification. For TNC questions, you need both advantages (jobs, tax revenue) AND disadvantages (oil spills, profit repatriation) with specific evidence.
introTips: Nigeria is an NEE — West Africa's largest economy; don't call it an LIC.
Shell's oil operations are the go-to TNC example — know both benefits and the environmental damage.
The north-south divide within Nigeria is an important inequality point for 6-mark answers.
intro: Nigeria is a country of extraordinary contrasts: Africa's most populous nation, one of its largest economies, home to vast oil reserves and the world's second-largest film industry by output (2009 ranking) — yet also a place where millions live on under $2 a day, where oil spills have poisoned farmland for generations, and where the gap between north and south, rich and poor, is vast. Nigeria's story shows both what rapid development can achieve and what it can cost.

keyPoints.heading: Nigeria in context
keyPoints.content: Nigeria is located in West Africa and is the continent's most populous country with over 220 million people (2023 estimate). Nigeria has one of Africa's largest economies, worth roughly $360–400 billion (2024 estimate), having been the continent's largest for most of the 2010s before currency devaluation cut its measured size. Nigeria is classified as an NEE (Newly Emerging Economy) — transitioning from a primarily agriculture-based economy towards industry and services. Nigeria has abundant natural resources: oil (Niger Delta — among the world's largest proven reserves, 2020s estimates), natural gas, coal, tin, iron ore, cocoa and palm oil. Its colonial history is significant: under British rule from 1861 to 1960, the British exploited groundnuts, palm oil and tin, and drew borders that cut across 250+ ethnic groups including the Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo. These divisions have caused ongoing political tensions.

One of Africa's largest economies — ~$360–400bn (2024 est.); the largest for most of the 2010s
NEE — Newly Emerging Economy; transitioning from agriculture to industry and services
Natural resources — oil (among the world's largest reserves), gas, coal, cocoa, palm oil

250+ ethnic groups — Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, Igbo — divisions persist

keyTerms.def: Newly Emerging Economy — a country whose economy is growing quickly as it industrialises, moving it out of the low income group. Nigeria, India and Brazil are examples.

When one country takes control of another and runs it for its own benefit. Britain ruled Nigeria from 1861 to 1960, taking out raw materials such as palm oil, groundnuts and tin, and drawing borders that cut across more than 250 ethnic groups.

Materials found in a country that can be used or sold — Nigeria's include crude oil, natural gas, tin and farmland. Having them does not automatically make a country rich; what matters is who controls them and where the money goes.

The huge wetland region in southern Nigeria where the River Niger meets the sea. Almost all of Nigeria's oil is produced here, and it is also where the worst pollution and the deepest local anger about oil are found.

keyPoints.memTip: Nigeria = Africa's most populous + most populous = pressure. Lots of people, lots of resources, lots of inequality.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The colonial legacy is important context for understanding Nigeria's development challenges — ethnic tensions and unfair trade patterns both trace back to this period.

keyPoints.heading: Nigeria's changing economy
keyPoints.content: In the 1960s, Nigeria's economy was primarily agricultural (cocoa, groundnuts). Oil was discovered in 1956 and by the 1970s had become dominant. Through the 2010s, oil made up over 90% of Nigeria's export earnings and roughly 70% of government revenue, though the revenue share swings with the oil price. However, oil employs only a small share of the workforce — often quoted as around 3%, though estimates vary — because it is capital-intensive (machines, not people, do the work), and volatile oil prices have caused economic boom and bust cycles. Manufacturing is growing in Lagos: Unilever, Nestlé and Cadbury all have factories there. The services sector is expanding rapidly — banking is growing, and Nollywood (Nigeria's film industry) was ranked the world's second-largest film industry by output after Bollywood (2009 ranking), and is estimated to be worth billions of dollars. A growing middle class — one projection puts it at 23 million households by 2030 — is driving consumer demand. Lagos is one of Sub-Saharan Africa's main financial hubs and a megacity.
writeBullets: Oil dominates — 90%+ of exports, ~70% of government revenue (2010s)
Oil employs only a small share of workers (often quoted ~3%) — capital-intensive, not labour-intensive
Volatile oil prices cause boom-bust economic cycles
Manufacturing growing — Lagos: Unilever, Nestlé, Cadbury factories
Nollywood — ranked world's 2nd largest film industry by output (2009); estimated multi-billion dollar industry
Growing middle class — one projection: 23m households by 2030
Lagos — megacity and one of Sub-Saharan Africa's main financial hubs

keyTerms.def: Relying on one export for most of a country's earnings. Oil makes up the large majority of Nigeria's export income, so when the world oil price falls, government income collapses with it.

An industry that needs huge amounts of money and machinery but relatively few workers. Oil is capital-intensive, which is why it earns Nigeria so much while employing only a small share of the workforce.
Nigeria's largest city and its commercial centre, on the southern coast. It is one of the fastest-growing cities in the world and generates a large share of the country's non-oil economy.
Nigeria's film industry, based mainly in Lagos. It produces more films per year than almost anywhere else in the world and is an example of Nigeria's economy growing beyond oil.
The growing group of Nigerians with steady incomes, some savings and spending power beyond basic needs. A rising middle class is one sign of an economy moving out of the low income group.

keyPoints.memTip: Oil earns the money but creates few jobs — Nigeria needs to diversify beyond oil.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The contrast between oil's share of export revenue (over 90% in the 2010s) and employment (often quoted as about 3%) is a powerful statistic to use in exam answers about uneven development.

keyPoints.heading: TNCs: Shell and others
keyPoints.content: TNCs (Transnational Corporations) play a major role in Nigeria's economy. Shell has operated oil extraction in the Niger Delta since 1958. Benefits of TNCs: government receives significant tax revenue and royalties; over 10,000 direct jobs created (an older, commonly quoted figure); infrastructure (roads, hospitals) was built near Shell facilities; technology transfer to local workers. Disadvantages: most profits are repatriated to the Netherlands and UK (Shell's home countries); relatively few local jobs given the industry's scale; environmental damage is severe. Estimates vary by source, but one commonly quoted range is 9–13 million barrels of oil spilled in the Niger Delta over the 50 years to the mid-2000s. The Bodo Creek spills (2008–9) reportedly contaminated around 69km² of creeks and farmland. How much oil was spilled is disputed: independent investigators' estimates, such as around 500,000 barrels, are far higher than Shell's own figures. Other TNCs include Unilever (consumer goods — soaps, food) and Diageo (Guinness Nigeria). Their presence brings technology transfer but raises questions about whether benefits reach ordinary Nigerians or primarily benefit shareholders abroad.

Government benefits — tax revenue and royalties from oil
Infrastructure built near Shell facilities — roads, hospitals
Profits repatriated to Netherlands/UK — most economic benefit leaves Nigeria
9–13m barrels estimated spilled over 50 years to the mid-2000s (varies by source) — severe pollution
Bodo Creek spills 2008–9 — spill volume disputed between Shell and independent investigators
Other TNCs — Unilever (soaps/food), Diageo (Guinness Nigeria)

keyTerms.def: Transnational Corporation — a company that operates in more than one country, usually with its headquarters in a wealthy country and its operations in others. Shell, Unilever and Coca-Cola all operate in Nigeria.
An oil company headquartered in the UK that has operated in Nigeria since the 1950s. It is the TNC most associated with both the money and the damage that oil has brought to the Niger Delta.

When a foreign company sends its profits back to its home country instead of reinvesting them where they were earned. It is the main reason a country can host a hugely profitable industry and stay poor.

A fishing community in the Niger Delta hit by two large oil spills in 2008 and 2009. Estimates of how much oil was spilled vary widely between Shell and independent investigators; Shell agreed a compensation settlement with the community in 2015.

The huge wetland region in southern Nigeria where the River Niger meets the sea. Almost all of Nigeria's oil is produced here, and it is also where the worst pollution and the deepest local anger about oil are found.

keyPoints.memTip: Shell drills deep — profits go far away, pollution stays in Nigeria.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The Bodo Creek spills are a specific, named example that lifts exam answers — but the spill volume is disputed between Shell and independent investigators, so present any figure as an estimate.

keyPoints.heading: Aid, trade and investment
keyPoints.content: Nigeria receives various forms of international economic engagement. The UK (through FCDO, formerly DFID) has provided bilateral aid to Nigeria, though the amount has reduced in recent years; recent focus has been on governance and girls' education. Chinese investment is growing rapidly: China has committed a reported $23 billion (2010s figure; totals vary by source) to Nigerian infrastructure including roads, railways, and the Abuja light rail — in exchange for oil access. This raises concerns about Nigeria accumulating debt to China. The IMF has attached structural adjustment conditions to its support — including reducing government subsidies and privatising state companies — which have been controversial. Fairtrade cocoa schemes (e.g., Divine Chocolate) attempt to return more money to farmers. Nigeria is a member of ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States), a regional trade bloc aimed at reducing trade barriers and increasing economic integration across 15 West African nations (2024 membership).
writeBullets: UK aid (FCDO) — focused on governance and girls' education; reducing in recent years
Chinese investment — a reported $23bn committed (2010s); roads, railways, Abuja light rail in exchange for oil
Risk of debt dependency on China — 'debt trap' concern
IMF structural adjustment — conditions: reduce subsidies, privatise state companies; controversial
Fairtrade cocoa — Divine Chocolate returns more money to farmers
ECOWAS — West African trade bloc, 15 nations (2024); reduces barriers, increases integration

keyTerms.def: Money, goods or expertise given by one country or organisation to another. Short-term emergency aid follows disasters; long-term development aid pays for things like schools, clinics and water supplies.

Large-scale spending by Chinese companies and the Chinese state on Nigerian roads, railways and power stations, usually in exchange for access to oil and other resources. It builds infrastructure fast, but often uses Chinese workers and leaves Nigeria in debt.
International Monetary Fund — an international organisation that lends money to countries in financial trouble, usually attaching conditions about how they run their economy.

Economic Community of West African States — a group of fifteen West African countries that trade with each other on favourable terms and allow free movement between member states. Nigeria is its largest member.
A scheme that guarantees farmers a minimum price for their crop plus an extra payment for their community, so growers rather than buyers keep more of the money.

keyPoints.memTip: China builds, UK funds schools, IMF sets conditions — three different types of international engagement.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Chinese investment is a nuanced topic — it brings infrastructure but may create debt dependency. Good for evaluation marks.

keyPoints.heading: Inequality and environmental issues
keyPoints.content: Nigeria's development is extremely uneven. The north (Hausa-Fulani Muslim majority) has lower literacy rates, more subsistence farming, and has been severely affected by the Boko Haram insurgency since 2009, which by some estimates has killed over 100,000 people (death-toll estimates vary widely) and has displaced more than 2 million (2020s estimate). The south (more development, oil wealth, Christian majority) has better infrastructure and higher incomes. Gender inequality persists: female literacy is around 55% versus 71% for males (2018 estimate). The contrast between Lagos and rural north-east Nigeria is one of the starkest development divides within any single country. Niger Delta oil spills have caused catastrophic environmental damage to the Ogoniland region. The Ogoni people, led by activist Ken Saro-Wiwa, protested Shell's pollution — Saro-Wiwa was executed by the Abacha military government in 1995, causing international outrage. A UNEP report (2011) estimated that cleaning up Ogoniland would take 30 years and cost $1 billion.
writeBullets: North-south divide — north: lower literacy, subsistence farming, Boko Haram insurgency
Boko Haram — 100,000+ killed by some estimates, 2m+ displaced since 2009 in north-east Nigeria
Gender inequality — female literacy ~55% vs male 71% (2018)
Ogoniland — oil pollution devastated farmland and fishing; UNEP 2011: 30-year cleanup needed
Ken Saro-Wiwa — Ogoni activist protested Shell pollution; executed 1995; international outcry
Natural gas flaring — wastes energy, emits CO₂, causes health problems for nearby communities
UNEP Ogoniland report (2011) — estimated $1bn and 30 years to clean up

keyTerms.def: Burning off the natural gas that comes up alongside crude oil, instead of capturing and using it. It wastes a valuable fuel, pollutes the air for people living nearby and adds to climate change.

An area of the Niger Delta, home to the Ogoni people, where decades of oil extraction left farmland and drinking water heavily contaminated. A United Nations study found the clean-up would take decades.

A Nigerian writer and campaigner who led a non-violent movement demanding that the Ogoni people share in oil wealth and that the pollution stop. He was executed by Nigeria's military government in 1995, which brought international attention to the Niger Delta.
An armed extremist group active in north-eastern Nigeria since 2009. Its violence has displaced millions of people and has made the north, already the poorer half of the country, poorer still.
The gap between what men and women can expect in education, work and income. In Nigeria it is much wider in the north than the south, where far fewer girls complete secondary school.

keyPoints.memTip: North struggles, south develops — and even in the oil-rich south, Ogoniland shows the environmental cost.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ken Saro-Wiwa is a powerful human story linking environmental damage, corporate accountability and human rights — use it in 6-mark evaluation questions.

2.question: What was the environmental impact of the Bodo Creek oil spill in 2008–9?
options: Creeks and farmland were contaminated, and how much oil was spilled is disputed between Shell and independent investigators
The spill was contained within days and left no lasting damage
The spill caused an explosion at the refinery, destroying 30km of pipeline
The oil entered Lagos harbour, closing the port for six months
2.correctFeedback: Correct! The Bodo Creek spills contaminated creeks and farmland in the Niger Delta. Independent estimates of the volume, such as around 500,000 barrels, are far higher than Shell's own figures. It's one of the most important specific examples of TNC environmental damage to know.
2.wrongFeedback: Not quite. The Bodo Creek spills (2008–9) contaminated creeks, farmland and fishing grounds in the Niger Delta. How much oil was spilled is disputed between Shell and independent investigators.

4.question: What did the UNEP Ogoniland report (2011) conclude about oil pollution in Nigeria?
options: That cleaning up Ogoniland would take approximately 30 years and cost $1 billion
That Shell had already begun a successful cleanup and the land would recover within 5 years
That the Nigerian government was solely responsible for the pollution, not Shell
That the pollution was exaggerated and most farmland was still productive
4.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The UNEP 2011 report on Ogoniland was damning — it estimated a 30-year cleanup costing $1 billion, highlighting just how severe the long-term damage from oil extraction has been.
4.wrongFeedback: That's not what UNEP found. The 2011 Ogoniland report concluded that cleanup would take approximately 30 years and cost around $1 billion — a devastating assessment of decades of oil pollution.

commonMistakes: Calling Nigeria an LIC — it is an NEE (Newly Emerging Economy) with one of Africa's largest economies. Poverty is due to inequality and poor distribution of wealth, not a lack of development overall.

Saying oil 'employs most Nigerians' — oil provided around 90% of export revenue in the 2010s but employs only a small share of workers (often quoted as about 3%) because it is capital-intensive (machines-led).
Forgetting to evaluate TNCs — always give both sides: jobs and infrastructure (benefits) AND profit repatriation and environmental damage (costs).
Not naming the Ogoni people or Ken Saro-Wiwa — these specific details push answers from Level 2 to Level 3 in extended writing.
Confusing Nigeria with Niger — Nigeria is the large NEE; Niger is a neighbouring LIC with very low development indicators. They are different countries.
examTips: For TNC questions, use the table structure: employment, income, infrastructure, environment, economic leakage — this ensures you cover advantages AND disadvantages systematically.
Name the Bodo Creek spills (2008–9), noting the spill volume is disputed, and quote UNEP's 2011 estimate (30 years, $1bn cleanup) — specific evidence signals a top-band answer.
For inequality questions, use the north-south divide within Nigeria — Boko Haram in the north vs oil wealth in the south — and link to colonial history (arbitrary borders).
The Ken Saro-Wiwa case links environmental damage to human rights — powerful material for 'assess the impact of TNCs' 9-mark questions.
